Preface
These are my personal notes compiled while studying probability and statistics at university. They combine the mathematical development of the material with worked examples and simulations in R.
The source for these notes lives on GitHub.

title: Probability & Statistics Notes
text:
How these notes are organized

Probability — foundational definitions, random variables, and standard distributions.
Statistical inference — estimation, hypothesis testing, and confidence intervals.
Regression & modeling — linear models and beyond.

Each chapter mixes theory (definitions, theorems, derivations) with R code used to illustrate or verify the results.

title: 1  Probability basics
text:
1.1 Sample spaces and events
A sample space \(\Omega\) is the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment. An event \(A\) is a subset of \(\Omega\), i.e. \(A \subseteq
\Omega\).
From these axioms it follows that for any two events \(A\) and \(B\),
\[
P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B).
\tag{1.1}\]
We use Equation 1.1 repeatedly in later chapters (e.g. when computing unions of overlapping events).

title: 1  Probability basics
text:
NoteDefinition: Probability measure



A probability measure \(P\) on \(\Omega\) satisfies:

\(P(\Omega) = 1\)
\(P(A) \geq 0\) for all events \(A\)
For disjoint events \(A_1, A_2, \dots\), \[
P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} P(A_i)
\]

title: 1  Probability basics
text:
1.2 Simulating a simple probability
Suppose we want to check the classic birthday problem: the probability that, among \(n\) people, at least two share a birthday. We can verify the closed-form result with a Monte Carlo simulation in R.

birthday_prob_sim <- function(n, trials = 10000) {
  hits <- replicate(trials, {
    birthdays <- sample(1:365, n, replace = TRUE)
    any(duplicated(birthdays))
  })
  mean(hits)
}

birthday_prob_theory <- function(n) {
  1 - prod((365 - 0:(n - 1)) / 365)
}

n_vals <- 2:50
sim <- sapply(n_vals, birthday_prob_sim)
theory <- sapply(n_vals, birthday_prob_theory)

plot(n_vals, theory, type = "l", col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Number of people", ylab = "P(shared birthday)")
lines(n_vals, sim, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
legend("bottomright", legend = c("Theoretical", "Simulated"),
       col = c("steelblue", "firebrick"), lty = c(1, 2))




Simulated vs. theoretical probability of a shared birthday




The simulated curve tracks the theoretical curve closely, confirming the complement-counting argument used to derive \(P(\text{no shared birthday}) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{365-i}{365}\).






TipExam tip



Whenever a problem asks for “at least one” of something, it’s usually easier to compute the complement \(P(\text{none})\) and subtract from 1.
